newsitem.title: USA: US pacts could hurt Central American airlines.
newsitem.headline: US pacts could hurt Central American airlines.

text.p: Open skies agreements being struck between the United States and Central American countries will make competition even tougher for those countries' cargo and passenger airlines, experts said.
"It will mean more competition and lower (cargo) rates for the Central American airlines," Rick Cashman, a consultant with MergeGlobal Inc, the Arlington, Virginia, air cargo consulting firm, said.

The United States is close to signing open skies agreements with several more Central American countries after inking a deal with Panama recently, Department of Transportation spokesman Bill Mosley said Friday.
Agreements are expected with Costa Rica, Honduras, El Salvador and Guatamala in "the next few weeks," Mosely said. The Panama agreement will be effective with the others as a group, Mosely said.
The discussions with all the countries are being held through the embassies there, he said.
"It has been a pretty rocky airfreight market," Brain Clancy, another MergeGlobal consultant, said. "The economies have been unstable."
"They have not developed the infrastructure for good service," Jose Aguirre, vice president, Miami International Forwarders, said Monday. "Maybe the open skies will help that," he said.
Central America "has and will continue to be the apparel assembly area for the United States," Clancy said.
But the consultants said the Central American countries already had liberal agreements with the United States, so the open skies would not produce a radically different air cargo market.
"Capacity is not a problem," Clancy said. "This is not going to be a situation where anyone is rushing to throw airplanes in there."
